Le rôle symbolique et historique du camp: The symbolic and historical role of the McGill encampment for Gaza
En recontextualisant le campement de McG: Placing the McGill encampment in historical context reveals the shades of grey in a debate too often painted in black and white.
Le 3 mai 2024, des manifestants pro-isra: On May 3, 2024, pro-Israeli demonstrators face pro-Palestinian demonstrators at the McGill University encampment in Montréal. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
New-York, Washington, Ottawa, Paris, Ber: New York, Washington, Ottawa, Paris, Berlin, Geneva, Mexico City, Sydney, Vancouver, Toronto… Starting at the prestigious Columbia University in the United States, an international movement of student mobilization for the Palestinian cause has spread since April 17. In Montréal, the McGill University encampment has become the meeting point for struggles for Gaza. On the fourteenth day of the occupation of the institution that trains Quebec’s elite, La Converse spoke with students, professors and researchers to better understand what is at stake in this mobilization and to put into context what some see as a new “May ’68.”
Au cœur de la métropole montréalaise, de: In the heart of the city, behind the imposing Roddick Gates that mark the main entrance to McGill University, an encampment in solidarity with the Palestinian people grows bigger by the day under the gaze of the business towers. On the lawn, finally green after a long winter, dozens of tents are sheltered behind metal fences covered with banners and signs: “You fund genocide,” “Profs for Palestine,” “McGill against austerity,” “Quebec doctors against the genocide in Gaza.”
Si les commentateurs et les chroniqueurs: While commentators and columnists rush to proclaim their opinions as immutable truths, pointing fingers at the good guys and the bad guys, those who are right and those who are wrong, it is crucial to step back. By speaking with pro-Israeli activists as well as their pro-Palestinian opponents, with Jewish and Muslim communities, with students and professors, and by placing the McGill encampment in historical context, we can see the shades of grey in a debate too often painted in black and white.
Les attaques menées par le Hamas le 7 oc: The attacks carried out by Hamas in Israel on October 7 cost 1,200 people their lives, including 37 children. To date, an estimated 125 people are still being held hostage, including 2 children, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). After seven months of Israeli bombardment of the Gaza Strip, 35,562 people are reported to have been killed, including 14,000 children and 9,000 women, according to UNICEF’s May 21 count. The UN agency estimates that <l1>a child is injured or killed every ten minutes in the Gaza Strip.</l1> This latest tragedy is part of a complex history of colonization and apartheid endured by the Palestinian people for more than seventy-five years.
L’armée israélienne a lancé l’assaut sur: The Israeli army launched its assault on Rafah on Monday, May 6, bombing the last refuge of 1.4 million Palestinians trapped in the south of the Gaza Strip – half of the enclave’s population, according to the UN. The decision has been widely condemned by international political leaders, including the United States, Israel’s longtime ally. Two days earlier, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also announced his refusal to sign a ceasefire agreement with Hamas.
À près de 9000 km du théâtre de cette of: Nearly 9,000 km from the theatre of this offensive in Gaza, Montréal students are on their twenty-sixth day of camping in front of Quebec’s oldest university. Applauded by some and decried by others, <l1>this new student movement </l1>is dividing Quebec society, part of which sees in it the “courage of youth,” and part of which sees “disguised” antisemitism.
Le campement pro-palestinien établi deva: The pro-Palestinian encampment set up in front of McGill University grows bigger by the day. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Très vite, quelques jours à peine après: Very quickly, barely a few days after the first night on April 27, a real organization took shape on campus, notably to cope with the rain that turned the park into a muddy field last week. “There’s a really beautiful solidarity from many Montrealers of all backgrounds and all ages, who brought us wooden pallets so we wouldn’t have to stay in the water, food, changes of clothes… In the current context of tension, it’s really nice,” says Camille, a Concordia student who joined the movement on the third day.
Au delà des considérations pratiques, ce: Beyond practical considerations, this coordination allows the various groups – including “McGill Hunger Strike for Palestine,” “Independent Jewish Voices” and “Students for Justice in Palestine” – and the individuals who make up the movement to speak with one and the same voice. This was notably the case at the press conference held in front of about ten journalists following an unsuccessful negotiation session with the administration on Monday, May 6. “We organize de-escalation trainings in case of outside provocations, workshops, discussions, screenings… Everyone has the chance to speak and we make all decisions collectively,” says Ari Neumann, a Jewish McGill student.
Une conférence de presse organisée par l: A press conference organized by students following a meeting with the McGill administration. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Perçus comme des « utopistes » par certa: Seen as “utopians” by some, or as “privileged people who don’t know what they’re talking about” by their pro-Israeli opponents, the campers have concrete demands for Montréal university administrations. “We know that McGill, like Concordia or UQAM, can’t decide on a ceasefire, and that’s not what we’re asking for. Our demands are clear: the boycott of, and financial divestment by, universities from companies that support Israel and the ongoing genocide in Gaza,” insists Ari Meumann.
Inspirés par leurs camarades américains,: Inspired by their American counterparts, the protesters have drawn up a list of companies, some of which work in the arms or national defence sector. “Their call for Montréal universities to divest is part of a strategy to make the issue local, because they are often accused of being too utopian. Here, they are anchoring their demands in something more concrete, something that affects people more directly, which will mobilize more students and prevent the university from answering that it can’t stop the war. McGill is the most compromised university in Quebec on this front,” explains Daniel Poitras, a historian and specialist in Quebec student movements.
En effet, l’université McGill a investi: Indeed, McGill University has invested more than $70 million in companies that support or contribute to Israel’s policies. Part of that budget is reportedly going directly to manufacturers of weapons and military technology with contracts with the Israeli army. Examples include Lockheed Martin, Thales, Safran, and even Bombardier. Other targeted companies supply fuel or communications equipment to the IDF.
Des étudiants réagissent aux prises de p: Students react to speeches on May 2, 2024, in front of the pro-Palestinian encampment at McGill. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
« C’est une question de moralité sur laq: “It’s a question of morality that we think it’s completely legitimate to ask about. We believe a university can’t just invest in anything and everything with our tuition money,” says Mehdi, a student. Last November, McGill students had already expressed their disagreement by voting more than 78% in favour of a Policy Against Genocide in a referendum organized by the solidarity group for Palestinian human rights. It was only five months later that the encampment was set up in situ.
« Nous écoutons leurs demandes et nous n: “We are listening to their demands and are striving to find concrete solutions consistent with our institution’s mission and principles,” the university said in a brief statement two weeks ago. For their part, the protesters are calling for the encampment to keep growing “for as long as the administration has not presented concrete measures and a timeline.” Galvanized by the victories won at some American universities – nearly a dozen of them have reached an agreement with mobilized students – and as new Canadian campuses join in, the McGill campers seem determined.
« Il est toujours difficile d’écrire l’h: “It is always difficult to write history as it is being made. In the eyes of the historian, a failed revolution is merely a riot; in the mouth of a reactionary power, it is normal to call the early signs of a revolution a riot,” wrote the late Guy Michaud in an article published in June 1968 in Le Monde diplomatique. A professor at Nanterre, the second-largest university in France, he had supported the student movement led notably by Daniel Cohn-Bendit, alongside other renowned academics such as sociologists Alain Touraine and Henri Lefebvre.
Un demi-siècle plus tard, ces mots réson: Half a century later, those words still resonate. “What we’re living through today can indeed call to mind what happened at the start of May ’68 in France; we have to watch how it evolves in the coming weeks,” cautions Daniel Poitras. It is indeed hard to anticipate the medium- and long-term effects of this new student mobilization. Still, it is rooted in a certain tradition of protest in the university world, while standing out in some respects. We are seeing a renewed interest and engagement among students for a cause playing out abroad, as well as active participation by the faculty.
La belle province a déjà vu fleurir plus: Quebec, la belle province, has seen a number of student protests blossom in the past. The first emerged in the mid-1950s. “A fairly little-known event took place in 1955: the first inter-university demonstration with a social aim in Quebec, against the increase in streetcar fares,” explains Daniel Poitras. “In 1958, there was the first day of student strike, inspired by what was being done in France, with big names like René Lévesque speaking to support the movement. At that time there was no trouble.”
Finalement, la fin des années soixante m: Finally, the late 1960s saw the first sit-ins in educational institutions. “The radicalization of student revolts happened above all through the CEGEPs, half of which were occupied in the fall to demand more rights, such as the creation of scholarships for students, or a second French-language university. That’s also when we see the internationalization of the student movement. That openness to international news remains timid, though (...). The war in Vietnam, which mobilized so many people in Europe or the United States, only mobilized 1,000 people at a march,” recalls the author of L'Université de Montréal. Une histoire urbaine et internationale. “What’s happening at McGill today is reawakening an international consciousness that had been asleep for some time.”
Marqué par un “enjeu de survivance” et u: Marked by a “question of survival” and a “feeling of isolation,” Quebec has tended to be late in becoming aware of certain international issues. But this has slowly changed over the past few decades.
De plus en plus de professeurs de l’univ: More and more university professors are joining the movement launched by their students. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
La participation de plus en plus visible: The increasingly visible and active participation of dozens of university professors in the current movement for Gaza illustrates this. “I’m Jewish, I grew up going to Jewish youth camps that praised Israel, but my studies allowed me to move beyond that single view; today, I teach at a university where students are taught history, sociology, critical thinking… It seems natural to me to stand with them when they apply what they’ve learned to defend Palestinians,” says <l1>Daniel Schwartz</l1>, an assistant professor of film at McGill University.
Selon lui, ils sont plus de 150 enseigna: According to him, more than 150 teachers have offered their support to the campers. Among them is Palestinian Nayrouz Abu Hatoum, an assistant professor of sociology and anthropology at Concordia: “It’s important to be here as professors because students are sacrificing a lot in their lives to be here and defend their convictions. It’s the least we can do so that they feel heard and legitimate in a context where there is a lot of gaslighting and opposition,” she says.
Illégalité et antisémitisme sont en effe: Illegality and antisemitism are indeed the two grounds put forward by those calling for the camp to be dismantled.
Comme à Science-Po Paris en France ou à: As at Sciences Po Paris in France or Columbia in the United States, McGill students are under fire. The administration, along with certain political figures such as Premier Legault, are calling for the encampment to be dismantled, arguing that the occupation is illegal.
« Les campus ont un rôle symbolique dans: “Campuses have a symbolic role in social awakenings because these are the future elite of Quebec, a social status that gives their words a certain legitimacy. Besides, as soon as students call out political figures, the latter are uncomfortable, even more so when it’s McGill, which is considered the crème de la crème,” analyzes Daniel Poitras.
Le campement de McGill n’a connu aucun d: The McGill encampment has seen no disorder and remains peaceful. Set up between two academic terms, it blocks neither access to nor the regular activities of the university. Even the police, often quick to intervene in the past, say they have had no problems with the protesters, who communicate with them regularly. A Quebec Superior Court judge, for her part, rejected the request for a provisional injunction filed by two students seeking the dismantling of the encampment, so as not to hinder freedom of expression.
Qu’à cela ne tienne, plusieurs organisat: Undeterred, several Zionist organizations responded by organizing a counter-demonstration a few metres from the pro-Palestinian encampment. Face to face, the demonstrators size each other up but do not understand each other. “We’re calling for it to be dismantled because these people want the death of all Jews around the world, when I’m more Arab than most of them,” said Myriam, a Jewish Montrealer of Moroccan origin.
Myriam, une Montréalaise de confession j: Myriam, a Jewish Montrealer, takes part in the pro-Israeli demonstration on May 2, 2024. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Une perception partagée par les quelque: A view shared by the roughly 200 demonstrators gathered to music on May 3, 2024, between screenings of images and testimonies from October 7 survivors on a giant screen. Ora Bar, a Concordia student, confirms: “We’re really here for unity and to show that we’re human beings and that encouraging our murder is not the way to get to peace.” The young woman has been very active since the start of the conflict. And for good reason: Ora Bar is one of the recipients of a scholarship offered by Honest Reporting Canada, a pro-Israeli lobby group. For this second edition, about twenty students, some of them in journalism programs like Ora Bar, received $1,000. In exchange, the student, who was born in Israel, commits to defending and spreading the Hebrew state’s propaganda on her social media and at the events she attends… She must also monitor the coverage of Israel in Concordia’s campus student media.
Un rôle qu’elle remplit également en rép: A role she also fills by giving media interviews. On the very day of this demonstration, Ora Bar is on the set of Radio-Canada’s TV show 24.60. The well-known host Anne-Marie Dussault introduces her as “a Jewish Israeli student at Concordia University in Montréal with a journalism degree, born in Israel and back in Quebec since the age of 11.” At no point is it mentioned that she was a recipient of the Honest Reporting Canada scholarship.
Pour savoir si l’antisémitisme est un en: To find out whether antisemitism is a concern within the encampment, we spoke with Ari Neueman, a Jewish student taking part in the pro-Palestinian encampment. The use of the word intifada in particular is singled out. “In Arabic it means uprising or revolt, it’s not a call to murder. The question of antisemitism within the movement was indeed raised, but not by the Jewish members. It was other groups who came to ask us whether we had faced that kind of problem, which we haven’t. As a precaution, we organized a discussion on the subject and we all agree that we oppose Zionism, not Judaism. They deliberately link religion to politics so that they can never be criticized,” she says.

L’antisionisme existe en effet depuis la: Anti-Zionism has indeed existed since the creation of the political movement aimed at establishing, and then consolidating, a Jewish state (the New Zion) in Palestine. In Montréal as in Israel, Jews who oppose the Hebrew state are often considered traitors. Their support for the pro-Palestinian movement, which would prove that the movement is not antisemitic by nature, is therefore waved away by pro-Israelis.
« Quand on regarde les insultes lancées: “When you look at the insults thrown at students demonstrating for Palestine, it’s antisemitism that comes up systematically. This reflex of using ostracizing labels is meant to invalidate the other person’s position. Before, students were called communists, now it’s antisemitism, since it’s the only thing that can be used against them,” deciphers Daniel Poitras.
L’heure n’est donc pas au dialogue tant: This is therefore no time for dialogue, so entrenched are the positions. The McGill campers have nonetheless managed to put Gaza back at the forefront of the media stage and to draw public attention, at a time when the demonstration held every Sunday for several months was losing steam. On May 20, Karim Khan, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, requested arrest warrants for three Hamas leaders as well as the Israeli prime minister and defence minister.
